items.q: In the Gartner survey of 186 ERP implementations, what proportion of **failed** projects did not use performance metrics?
items.explain: **70% of failed projects did not use performance metrics**, and a separate **27% did not measure at all**. Do not confuse these with the **<25% that deliver hard monetary benefits**. The measurement finding is why *"results to be measurable"* is a BPR key to success.

items.q: An organization is described in the deck as an integration of which three things?
items.explain: **People, Process & Technology** — the classic triangle, with the goal of aligning all three being to **realize benefits**. Change one corner and you are obliged to change the other two, which is why an ERP rollout cannot be a purely technical project.

items.q: Which question is listed **first** in both the deck and the QnA as a reason people resist change?
options: Can I cope with new technologies?
What will be my new role?
items.explain: **"What's in it for me?" (WIIFM).** It is worth noting the question is *reasonable*: the twelve ERP benefits accrue to the **organization**, while the individual clerk gets more fields to fill in. The resistance reflects a genuine asymmetry, which is why the remedy is **incentives and new roles**, not persuasion.

items.q: In the two-level strategy for handling change, what is named as the **key** for the second level (getting motivated and committed)?
items.explain: **Organizational design** is the key to Level 2; **communication** is the key to Level 1. The levels are a ladder — Level 1 removes fear, Level 2 builds commitment — and **you cannot skip to Level 2, because a frightened employee cannot be motivated**.

items.q: Which is stated as the **basic objective of Organizational Design**?
options: To reduce headcount in line with the new process
The architecture of the organization needs to be aligned with the new process and technology
To define job descriptions for every role
items.explain: **"The architecture of the organization needs to be aligned with the new process and technology."** The word *architecture* is deliberate — you cannot install a new process into an incompatible structure any more than you can add a floor to a building not designed to carry it.

items.q: The Core Change Team is drawn primarily from which function?
options: HR, OD professionals and/or the consulting team
items.explain: **HR, OD professionals and/or consulting team** — dedicated resources, ideally a **mix of long and short-term employees**. Note the **Extended** Change Team is the one drawn part-time from **line management**. Both are *generally not part of the primary implementation team*.

items.q: When do change management actions happen in an ERP project?
items.explain: **All throughout.** The deck poses this as an explicit question. Change management is a **workstream, not a phase** — the same structure as Ascendant's **Organization** workstream running across all seven phases.

items.q: Which phase does the deck call **critical from a change management perspective**?
items.explain: **Go Live** — *"some people may literally **feel helpless** if applications they are used to is withdrawn."* A competent, fluent employee becomes a beginner overnight, which is why *"address the impact of withdrawal of legacy systems"* is a listed activity and why the **parallel run** is a change-management instrument as much as a technical safeguard.

items.q: In ASAP's six change management processes, which one is described as **spanning across the other five**?
items.explain: **Communications** — *"communication spans across the other 5, but has its own focus as well."* Every other process produces something that must be communicated, yet the strategy, framework and channels are work in their own right, which is why a **point person** is assigned to it.

items.q: ASAP defines **Assessment** as which of the following?
options: Aligning jobs and processes with the new business environment
items.explain: **Uncovering and prioritizing risks** — and specifically *"identify and prioritize handling of **perception**."* It is risk assessment applied to **people**, running the same identify → analyse → prioritize shape as Unit 1's risk management. The other three options are Sponsorship, Knowledge Transfer and Organizational Optimization respectively.

items.q: Hammer's definition of reengineering names four measures of performance. Which set is correct?
items.explain: **Cost, quality, service, and speed.** The full definition: *"a **fundamental rethinking** and **radical redesign** of business processes to achieve **dramatic improvements** in critical, contemporary measures of performance — such as cost, quality, service, and speed."*

items.q: Which of the four business process principles is the one that makes BPR possible?
options: It has a number of steps
Each step has specific input and output
Each step can be run by a separate organizational entity
Each step should add value to the whole process
items.explain: **"Each step should add value to the whole process."** It is a **test you can apply** — a step that adds no value is a candidate for elimination — and it generates the whole **Value Added / Non-Value Added / Waste** classification in the diagnosis phase.

items.q: According to the deck, which kind of organization is a **potential candidate for BPR**?
options: One that has been running stable for a while without much organizational change
One that has just implemented an ERP
items.explain: **"Any organization which has been running stable for a while without much organizational changes is a potential candidate for BPR."** Counter-intuitive but logical: four of the five forces driving BPR are **external**, so a process decays as the world moves even when nobody does anything wrong. **Stability is the warning sign.**

items.q: What does the deck identify as the fatal flaw in 1990s **downsizing**?
options: It was too expensive to implement
It required IT that did not yet exist
The value of resources, especially human, was under-estimated
It was applied only to manufacturing companies
items.explain: **"Value of resources, especially Human, was under-estimated, and the indirect impact on company image and credibility."** Downsizing correctly diagnosed **accumulated non-value-adding activity** but applied the wrong instrument — it removed **people** when the problem was **process**. That gap is what BPR filled.

items.q: Within what timeframe do the BPR keys to success say you should **show early success**?
items.explain: **Within the first three to six months.** This is a hard constraint, not a morale exercise — BPR's own con is that it *"can take long time"*, and an initiative showing nothing for two years **loses its sponsor**, which triggers failure reason 8. It is why *"potential for quick results"* is a process-selection factor.

items.q: "Too much AS IS analysis (paralysis)" is a reason BPR fails. What is the correct depth for AS-IS modelling?
options: Fully detailed, since it is the baseline for measurement
High level only — why the process exists, what it does, its high-level objective
As detailed as the TO-BE model
items.explain: **High level only** — *"no need of much detailed analysis as anyway the process will not be used in future."* The rule is **AS-IS shallow, TO-BE deep**. But *shallow on detail* does not mean careless: the **rules and assumptions** must still be documented, because they are what diagnosis interrogates.

items.q: Which proverb does the deck use to warn against automating an unchanged process?
options: Old process + new technology = costly old process
One can take the horse to the water
items.explain: **"Old process + new technology = costly old process."** Automating an unchanged bad process makes it **faster and more expensive**, not better — which is failure reason 5, *little change in process, not redesign*. (The other three quotes are all from this course too, but address data quality, motivation and benchmarking respectively.)

items.q: Which BPR team role is described as the **"conscience keeper of the leader"**?
items.explain: **The Change Coordinator.** The Leader drives toward *radical* and *dramatic* outcomes and is therefore most likely to push past what the organisation can absorb; the Change Coordinator **tests and reports periodically the reactions of the rest of the folks**. Note the **Reengineering** Coordinator handles the *"hard"* part — the two coordinators split the technical and human sides.

items.q: Which duty belongs to the **Process Owner** rather than the Leader?
options: Identifies the key business processes of the organization
Establishes measures of performance and rewards
Supports and protects radically new ideas
Articulates and communicates the need to reengineer
items.explain: **"Supports and protects radically new ideas"** is the Process Owner's. A radical proposal is fragile and needs shielding long enough to be evaluated, or the organisation regresses to tinkering. The other three are the **Leader's** duties — and note the Leader is described as **the Project Manager**.

items.q: Which is **not** one of the three decision factors for selecting a process to reengineer?
items.explain: **Lowest implementation cost** is not a stated factor. The three are **benchmarking** (an external yardstick), **unsatisfactory/troubled** (internal), and **potential for quick results** (political — it operationalises the *show early success in 3–6 months* key).

items.q: The deck cautions that non-value-adding activities should not simply be deleted. Why?
options: They are required by the ERP package
They may have some value, such as management information, which must be retained or transferred
Removing them requires steering committee approval
They are the only steps the customer sees
items.explain: *"Even though most of these do not add value, they **may have some value such as management information**. One needs to separate this and **retain / transfer this in some other step**."* An inspection may be the only place a quality metric is captured; a reconciliation may be statutory. **Non-value-adding is not the same as useless.**

items.q: In the Case Manager example, how many departments does the single case manager replace?
items.explain: **Four** — *Financing, Credit checking, Approval, Issuance* collapse into one **Case manager**. With them go **three hand-offs**, their queues, and the reconciliation between four departments' records. It is only possible because **IT** gives one person the information those four used to hold.

items.q: Why must the six levers of process redesign be moved in stages rather than all at once?
options: Because the steering committee approves them one at a time
Because they are interdependent, so the system must stabilize between shifts
Because the ERP can only be configured incrementally
Because each lever belongs to a different department
items.explain: **They are interdependent.** *"Set the levers in 1-2-2 state, stabilize the system; shift to higher levels 3-4-4… stabilize there."* Multi-skilling needs training; a flattened hierarchy needs the new roles to exist; process-level measurement needs the process to be running. Same staged logic as the **Rollout** deployment strategy.

items.q: In the BPR vs TQM comparison, what is TQM's **starting point**?
items.explain: **The existing process** — whereas BPR starts from a **clean slate**. This row follows directly from *fundamental rethinking*: a change that starts from the existing process cannot be a fundamental rethink. Remember the graph: **TQM is a slope, BPR is a step**, and every row of the table follows from that shape.

items.q: What is named as BPR's **primary enabler** in the comparison with TQM?
items.explain: **Information Technology** — TQM's primary enabler is **statistical control**. This is why *BE = BPR + IT*, and why IT is called *disruptive*: it removes the constraints (information locked in one place, expertise locked in one person) that shaped the old processes.

items.q: What is the stated risk of doing a **full-blown BPR before** ERP implementation that most directly creates gaps?
options: It takes a long time and cost
There is no guarantee the best-designed processes will be supported by the ERP solution
Business dynamics may change over three to four years
items.explain: **No guarantee the ERP will support the designed processes.** Every difference then becomes a **gap** that must be closed by **customization** — the central risk of Realization. Full-blown BPR before ERP manufactures exactly the problem gap analysis is meant to minimise. The other three are real risks too, but this is the one that produces gaps.

items.q: Which company is paired with **Vendor Managed Inventory (VMI)** in the benchmarking exemplars?
items.explain: **Wal-Mart — VMI.** The set to memorise: **Toyota — Just-in-Time (JIT)**, **Motorola — Six Sigma**, **Wal-Mart — VMI**. Toyota's **Kanban/JIT** and Wal-Mart's **VMI** are also named as best practices that arrived inside ERP packages *from leading corporations*.

items.q: Which thumb rule of process modelling most directly prevents reproducing the existing hand-offs?
options: Each process should have specific inputs and outputs
Focus on goals more than means
Assume no organizational structure or boundaries
Processes should relate to customers and their needs
items.explain: **"Assume no organizational structure or boundaries"** (with *"think outside all constraints"*). If you draw the To-Be process **as departments currently exist**, you reproduce the current hand-offs, because the boundaries generate them. **The org chart must not be an input to the process design.**

items.q: Place these in the correct order of the business process hierarchy, from Level 1 to Level 4.
items.explain: **Scenario → Process → Activity → Step (SPAS).** The deck's worked example: **Supply Chain Management → Order Management → Delivery Scheduling → Calculation of Delivery Date.** The hierarchy exists because *"business processes can be many"* — 40 to 100 even in a medium-sized company.

items.q: SCOR is based on five distinct management processes. Which is the correct set?
items.explain: **Plan · Source · Make · Deliver · Return.** *Source → Make → Deliver* is the physical flow, **Return** is the reverse flow, and **Plan** sits *above* the other four. The four operational processes **repeat at every link** of the chain, from **suppliers' supplier to customer's customer**.

items.q: BPMN maps to which execution language?
items.explain: **BPEL — Business Process Execution Language.** This is the most consequential fact about BPMN: a diagram is not only a picture but can be **mapped to constructs of an execution language and run**, which closes the gap between *business process design* and *implementation* — and means the model cannot go stale.

items.q: Which organization has maintained **BPMN** since 2005?
items.explain: **OMG** — BPMN was developed by **BPMI**, which merged with OMG in **2005**. Keep the three straight: **EPC → IDS Scheer → ARIS → SAP**; **BPMN → BPMI, then OMG → BPEL**; **UML → Rational Software → RUP** (and UML is for *software object modelling*, not business processes).

items.q: Roughly how many processes does the deck say even a **medium sized** company has?
items.explain: **40–100.** This is the number that justifies both **tools** (*"designing the processes is both tedious and error prone"*) and the **SPAS hierarchy** (*"business processes can be many, hence…"*). Flat, that many processes cannot be navigated or kept consistent.

items.q: What distinguishes a specialist tool such as ARIS from Visio for process modelling?
options: ARIS has basic business-process knowledge, while Visio's semantic support is very limited
ARIS is the only tool that can export to an ERP
items.explain: *"Even the simple tool Visio can be used to create business process models, **but the semantic support is very limited** — it is used only from a diagramming point. But the niche products such as **ARIS have basic BP knowledge**."* Visio draws boxes; ARIS understands that a box is a *process* and can therefore **validate** the model.

items.q: What does a **Business Model** show that a Business Process Model does not?
options: The steps and data flows of a process
Which organizational entity runs each step
The future application landscape, including where legacy applications will remain
items.explain: **The future application landscape** — *which processes ERP will take care of, **where legacy applications will remain**, and how data will flow between ERP modules and those legacy applications.* BPM models **one process**; BM models **the whole enterprise as one large system**, and it is the only artefact that shows the **boundary of the ERP**.
